# Methods and Results Draft

*Generated by `src/08_paper_outputs.py` from `results/tables/`. Do not edit numbers by hand; rerun the pipeline instead.*

## Research statement
From a person's recorded lifestyle and medical history, how well can we estimate the broad cause of death, and how much does the estimate suffer when parts of the record are missing?

## Data and cohort
We used structured decedent metadata from three data carts of the New Mexico Decedent Image Database (NMDID), eight linked tables per cart: 1500 rows, 1457 unique decedents after de-duplication, and 1450 adults after excluding 6 people under 18 and 1 with missing age. The 43 decedents present in two carts have identical records in every linked table (324 of 324 table-level comparisons), so cart extraction selects people without altering their records.

## Outcomes
1. **Primary, broad cause (n = 1380):** natural cardiac (373), drug or alcohol (500), injury (507). Excluded: 39 cardiac deaths with a non-natural manner and 31 other causes.
2. **Secondary, intent within injury deaths (n = 487):** accident, homicide, suicide.
3. **Negative control (n = 137):** stab versus gunshot homicides.

## Inputs and the eight sections of a record
Inputs were built as nested sets: M0, age and sex (2 inputs); M1, M0 plus lifestyle (drinking, tobacco, drug use, marital status, cadaver and living body mass index, education, socioeconomic status, diet, heavy lifting, firearm-access occupation; 60 inputs); M2, M1 plus 18 diagnoses and four lifetime injury or surgery items (87 inputs). Every block has a flag saying whether the investigator recorded it. The blocks form eight sections: drinking, tobacco, drug use, marital status, body size, social background, diagnoses, and past injuries and surgery. Seventeen administrative, geographic and post-mortem columns are blocked from every model and checked at build time; the source cart alone has Cramér's V 0.97 with the broad cause. Cadaver body mass index uses autopsy weight and length with only an implausibility filter, because blanking it for decomposition copies a blocked post-mortem variable into its flag (Cramér's V 0.74). Medications (partly scene evidence) and race and ethnicity are never in M0 to M2; they appear only in the accuracy-ceiling and subgroup analyses.

## Missing information
A section can be in three states: recorded; left blank by the investigator; or not available to the model. We compared five ways of handling a section that is not available: (1) present it as left blank; (2) fill in the typical value of the training fold; (3) multiple imputation by nearest-neighbour hot-deck, in which three donors drawn from the ten training people most similar on the available inputs supply the hidden sections and the predictions are averaged; (4) a single **withholding-trained model**, fitted on the training fold plus five copies in which every section is hidden independently with probability 0.15, 0.3, 0.5, 0.75 or 1.0, where a hidden section has its values and its flag removed and a separate indicator set, so that "not recorded" and "not available" stay distinct; and (5) a dedicated model refitted without the hidden sections, as a reference. Hiding is applied only to held-out people, after the models are fitted. The withholding-trained model's probabilities were recalibrated by temperature scaling learned on one fifth of each training fold, which never changes its answers. To choose the next question, the model ranks the sections a person is missing by the expected reduction in its uncertainty (entropy) over the three causes, averaging over plausible answers taken from training people of each cause and weighted by the current probability of that cause; neither the person's true cause nor their true answers are used. We compared this order with one fixed order for everyone and a random order, starting every held-out person from age and sex only.

## Validation and statistics
All estimates come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation repeated 5 times (seed 42), with each person's held-out probabilities averaged over repeats. Imputation and scaling are fitted inside training folds. Models are gradient boosting (main), random forest and logistic regression with fixed settings, plus their unweighted average. We report accuracy, macro one-vs-rest AUC, balanced accuracy, macro F1 and the multi-class Brier score with 95% intervals from 1000 bootstrap resamples of people; comparisons use the same resamples and are paired. The accuracy ceiling adds a nested search of tree size (inner 3-fold, log-loss) inside every outer training fold. Calibration uses decile reliability curves, expected calibration error and calibration slope. Shortlists use split conformal prediction with the score 1 minus the probability of the true cause, averaged over 500 random calibration and evaluation halves, in marginal, class-conditional and missingness-conditional versions (one threshold per band of blank sections). To check that the results carry over, models were also trained on deaths up to 2014 and tested on deaths from 2015 on, and trained on four groups of counties and tested on the fifth (five groups; the largest county formed its own group). Shortlist thresholds for later years were set on 2014 deaths with a model trained on deaths up to 2013. Year and county only defined these splits and were never model inputs. Analyses used Python 3.11.9 with scikit-learn 1.9.1, pandas 3.1.0, NumPy 2.4.6, statsmodels 0.15.0 and SHAP 0.51.0.

## Results

**Accuracy.** With all inputs, gradient boosting named the correct broad cause for 58.6% (55.8 to 61.2) of held-out people (macro AUC 0.776 (0.756 to 0.794)), against 51.3% (48.8 to 53.8) from age and sex alone and 36.7% for always naming the largest group. Lifestyle raised accuracy by +4.6 points (+1.9 to +7.8) and all inputs by +7.2 points (+4.1 to +10.2). The true cause was among the two most probable for 87.7% of people (84.1% with age and sex alone). Random forest reached 56.7%, logistic regression 56.5% and their average with gradient boosting 57.5%. Recall was 60.1% for cardiac, 57.6% for drug or alcohol and 58.4% for injury deaths. Intent within injury deaths stayed hard: 38.8% (34.1 to 43.3) with age and sex and 46.0% (41.5 to 50.3) with all inputs (best macro AUC 0.616, Ensemble). The highest accuracy any honest configuration reached was 62.0% (59.4 to 64.5) (M2 + medications + race and ethnicity, HistGB, nested search), +3.4 points (+0.9 to +5.9) over the main model. Across sex, age, race and ethnicity groups accuracy ranged from 53.7% (age 40-59) to 68.6% (sex Female).

**Later years and other regions.** Trained on deaths up to 2014 and tested on 493 deaths from 2015 on, the standard model named the correct cause for 58.0% (53.7 to 62.3) (macro AUC 0.770 (0.738 to 0.805)), close to the cross-validated 58.6%. Held-out groups of counties gave 57.2% (54.5 to 59.9) (macro AUC 0.756 (0.736 to 0.776)), ranging from 54.1% to 65.4% across the five groups. With every section hidden, the withholding-trained model again outperformed the naive handling, both in later years (51.1% versus 43.0%) and in other regions (50.7% versus 41.7%). On complete records in later years it was less accurate than the standard model (52.1% versus 58.0%), so the standard model remains the choice when a record is complete. Shortlists targeting 90% contained the true cause for 93.5% of later-year deaths with thresholds set on 2014 deaths (average length 2.35).

**Records as they are.** For people with no section left blank the standard model was correct for 58.6% (n = 140); for people with seven or eight sections blank, 55.1% (n = 486), where age and sex alone gave 54.9%. Accuracy does not fall steadily with missingness, because which sections are blank itself differs by cause of death.

**Same people, less information.** Hiding one section from the withholding-trained model cost at most 3.4 points (Drinking). With every section hidden, presenting the gaps as investigator blanks gave 42.9% (40.2 to 45.5), typical values gave 47.8% (45.2 to 50.4), and the withholding-trained model gave 52.8% (50.0 to 55.3), a difference of +9.9 points (+6.5 to +13.3) over the naive handling and +1.4 points (+0.0 to +3.0) against a model trained on age and sex alone. Multiple imputation gave 49.4% (47.0 to 52.1); the withholding-trained model differed from it by +3.3 points (+1.2 to +5.4). With all lifestyle sections hidden, the four handlings gave 49.6% (left blank), 50.7% (typical values), 51.0% (multiple imputation) and 52.7% (withholding-trained). With four random sections hidden, accuracy was 51.7% with the naive handling, 52.9% with multiple imputation and 52.9% with the withholding-trained model (curve values are means over single cross-validation repeats, because the hidden sections differ between repeats; all other estimates average each person's probabilities over the five repeats). On complete records the withholding-trained model matched the standard model (58.2% versus 58.6%; difference -0.4 points (-2.2 to +1.4)).

**Reliability.** Expected calibration error of the standard model was 0.034 to 0.041 across classes (calibration slope 0.78 to 0.89). Answering only when the top probability was at least 0.7 gave an answer for 32.7% of people with accuracy 72.1% (67.6 to 76.1). Shortlists targeting 90%, 95% and 99% contained the true cause for 90.0%, 95.0% and 99.2% of people, with average lengths of 1.99, 2.31 and 2.69 of the three causes; 20.4% of the 90% shortlists named a single cause. Marginal 90% coverage by true cause ranged from 89.5% to 90.7%; the class-conditional version gave 90.0% to 90.2%. With one threshold for everyone, 90% shortlists covered 86.4% to 92.4% of people across bands of blank sections; adjusting the threshold for the number of blank sections gave 90.0% to 91.1%.

**Why the estimate survives missing information.** A model that saw only which lifestyle sections were filled in recovered 61% of the lifestyle AUC gain; a model that saw only the recorded content, with the blank pattern destroyed, recovered at least 35% (lifestyle plus medical history: 58% and 36%; with logistic regression 67% and 8%). Among the 243 people with drinking, tobacco and diagnoses all recorded, all inputs changed AUC by +0.010 (-0.039 to +0.062). 38 of 85 factors differed by broad cause after FDR correction and 30 of 77 modelled factors after adjustment for age and sex (intent: 2 of 83 and 3 of 49). The inputs with the largest held-out SHAP values were age_years, drink_high_risk, dx_missing, cadaver_bmi, dx_hypertension, male, drug_missing, drink_missing.

**Controls.** In the negative control, logistic regression gave AUC 0.649 (0.532 to 0.765) with age and sex, and all inputs changed it by -0.028 (-0.128 to +0.067) (gradient boosting +0.022 (-0.070 to +0.109)). With shuffled labels the AUC was 0.498 (95% range 0.470 to 0.520; 20 shuffles) for the broad cause, against 0.767 with real labels on the same single-repeat setup (17 standard deviations; p = 0.0476, the smallest attainable), and 0.498 (0.328 to 0.624; 200 shuffles) for the negative control, against 0.612 (p = 0.0647). All-input macro AUC was 0.778 with decomposition-blanked body mass index, 0.772 with living body mass index only, 0.774 with class weights, 0.774 excluding deaths after 2017 and 0.776 with the cardiac-conflict ingestion deaths relabelled; adding zip code changed it by +0.007 (-0.001 to +0.015). Within cart 2966 (423 people) the gain over age and sex was +0.032 (-0.039 to +0.099). With every section hidden, the withholding-trained model reached 52.8%, 50.0%, 52.4% under the three withholding designs tested (default: rates 0.15, 0.3, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0; single rate 0.5; no fully hidden copy: rates 0.15 to 0.75), against 42.9% for the standard model with the gaps presented as blanks. A model given the blocked cart variable alone would reach 98.2%, which shows why that variable is blocked: any accuracy near that level on these data would come from how the carts were assembled, not from the person.

## Supplementary results
**Which question to ask next.** Starting from age and sex only, asking the section the model chose first gave 50.4%, against 48.4% with one fixed order and 50.3% with a random order; after two questions the figures were 52.0%, 50.4% and 51.4% (model-chosen minus random: +0.9 points (-1.1 to +3.3); model-chosen minus fixed: +3.4 points (+1.6 to +5.2)). The section most often asked first was body size (BMI) (47.9% of people). Curve values are means over single repeats.

**Recalibration.** Temperature scaling (mean temperature 2.21) changed the calibration slope of the withholding-trained model from between 0.58 and 0.68 (too confident) to between 1.22 and 1.41 (too cautious), and its expected calibration error from 0.053-0.064 to 0.047-0.055, without changing any answer; it overcorrects, so we do not use it by default.

## Limitations
1. **Ceiling of the data.** No honest configuration we tested exceeded 62.0% accuracy for three broad causes; accuracy near 98.2% appeared only when the blocked cart variable was used, which reflects how the carts were assembled rather than the person.
2. **Not a living-person tool.** Every person in NMDID died suddenly or violently and was investigated; predicting the eventual cause of death of living people needs a prospective cohort with follow-up.
3. **Investigation-driven records.** Inputs and outcome come from the same investigation, and which sections are blank differs by cause; part of the accuracy reflects this recording pattern, quantified in the explanation analysis.
4. **Cart design.** Each cart was drawn for one cause; identical duplicate records show extraction does not change records, but further selection when the carts were assembled cannot be excluded, and the within-cart check is small.
5. **Simulated missingness.** Hidden sections are hidden completely at random; real gaps in other settings may follow other patterns.
6. **Small groups.** The negative control has 137 people, intent and subgroup analyses are modest, and conformal coverage is averaged over random halves of one cohort.
7. **No validation outside NMDID.** Later years and other New Mexico regions are still one database and one office; settings were fixed except in the ceiling analysis.
